What it is, in one line: The rule that all data is made of three-part sentences: subject, predicate, object
What it does: Lets you add any new fact without changing a schema. 'Cetaphil contains Phenoxyethanol' is one triple
Why, or why not: It is what an ontology is written in. No choice here

What it is, in one line: The readable way of writing RDF
What it does: Our ontology file. Diffs cleanly in git
Why, or why not: Readable by humans, which the other formats are not

What it is, in one line: RDF plus real logic
What it does: Lets you say 'a sensitive-safe product is any product with no allergens' and have software work out who qualifies
Why, or why not: The defined classes need it. This is what makes it an ontology and not a spreadsheet

What it is, in one line: The query language for graphs. SQL for RDF. Say 'sparkle'
What it does: Answers questions like 'oily skin, no allergens, under $20, in Beirut'. Abesova, bit-Tech, TOXIN and FoodKG all use it
Why, or why not: Our 15 competency questions are each one SPARQL query

What it is, in one line: If-then rules for what OWL cannot say
What it does: OntoCosmetic writes its formulation rules in it. 'If product has a declarable allergen then not for sensitive skin'
Why, or why not: Only for two rules. It slows reasoning, and HermiT ignores it silently, so we would switch to Openllet

What it is, in one line: Checks the data obeys rules. OWL says what follows, SHACL says what MUST be true
What it does: 'Every product must have exactly one brand.' Our validate_dataset.py, moved onto the graph
Why, or why not: OWL assumes anything unsaid might be true, so it cannot enforce. SHACL can

What it is, in one line: A file that says 'this column becomes this property'. R2RML is for databases, RML adds CSV, YARRRML is RML in readable YAML
What it does: TOXIN used R2RML to turn Excel into a graph. This is how our CSV becomes triples
Why, or why not: A mapping file goes in the appendix and can be audited. A script cannot

What it is, in one line: The free desktop editor from Stanford. Everyone uses it
What it does: Build classes by clicking, press the reasoner button, screenshot the hierarchy. Moe, OntoCosmetic, Hansanie and COPPER all used it
Why, or why not: Standard, and reasoners are built in. But keep the Turtle file in git as the real master

What it is, in one line: A Python library for ontologies
What it does: Load the ontology, add facts, run a reasoner from code. Hansanie & Silva used it
Why, or why not: Our whole pipeline is Python

What it is, in one line: A Python library for plain RDF and SPARQL
What it does: Read and write triples, run queries, from Python
Why, or why not: Same reason. Pairs with Owlready2

What it is, in one line: A drawing tool for ontology modules, made for the MOMo method
What it does: Draw the module, get the OWL
Why, or why not: Nice for the diagrams the chapter needs. Not essential

What it is, in one line: Python's basic window toolkit
What it does: Hansanie & Silva built their desktop app with it
Why, or why not: We are not building a desktop app

What it is, in one line: A reasoner. Reads the ontology and works out what follows, and finds contradictions
What it does: Fills the defined classes. Flags the 593 sensitive-skin products that contain an allergen
Why, or why not: Ships with Protégé, solid default. Does NOT run SWRL rules

What it is, in one line: Another reasoner. Openllet is the maintained version
What it does: Same job, but it also runs SWRL rules. Hansanie & Silva used Pellet
Why, or why not: Only if we write SWRL rules

What it is, in one line: A very fast reasoner for a simple subset of OWL
What it does: Used by the big biomedical ontologies
Why, or why not: Too limited for our defined classes

What it is, in one line: A database for triples with SPARQL on the front and a picture of the graph
What it does: Stores our 1.8 million triples in named boxes per source. Abesova used it
Why, or why not: Free desktop edition, reasoning built in, and the visual explorer is worth more in a meeting than any paragraph

What it is, in one line: A free, simpler triple store
What it does: Same job as GraphDB. bit-Tech used it
Why, or why not: Simpler, but its reasoning is weak and it has no visual explorer. GraphDB does more for the same price

What it is, in one line: Commercial triple stores. Virtuoso runs DBpedia itself
What it does: Same job, bigger scale
Why, or why not: We do not need the scale and Stardog costs money

What it is, in one line: A point-and-click tool inside GraphDB that turns a CSV into triples
What it does: Abesova's team used it to map Sephora columns to classes
Why, or why not: Good, but the mapping is trapped inside GraphDB. Morph-KGC's mapping is a file we can put in the appendix

What it is, in one line: The Python engine that reads an RML mapping and writes the triples
What it does: One command turns our CSV into the graph. Rerun it whenever the data changes
Why, or why not: Python, fast on big CSVs, and the mapping is auditable. This is our population tool

What it is, in one line: The vocabulary Google uses for products and shops
What it does: Gives us Product, Offer, price, brand, seller. Splits the product from the offer, which is how one lotion holds two prices
Why, or why not: Everyone understands it already. No point inventing our own word for 'price'

What it is, in one line: A W3C standard for saying where information came from
What it does: wasAttributedTo, wasDerivedFrom, generatedAtTime. Our four evidence levels in a language other people speak
Why, or why not: Turns our most original design choice into a standard one. O'Sullivan 2025 did exactly this

What it is, in one line: For lists of words that are labels, not objects
What it does: Our benefits: 'Hydrating' and 'Hydration' become one concept with two labels
Why, or why not: Benefits are terms people use, not logical classes

What it is, in one line: The basic bookkeeping vocabulary: title, creator, licence, date
What it does: Makes the dataset and ontology citable
Why, or why not: Cheap and expected

What it is, in one line: The European Commission's official cosmetic ingredient register, 28,573 entries
What it does: Our ingredients get a legal status from it. Already linked on 99.2% of products with a formula
Why, or why not: It is the whole point

What it is, in one line: CosIng already converted to RDF, on GitHub
What it does: Could be our entire ingredient layer for free
Why, or why not: If usable, we cite it and save weeks. If not, our own conversion is a contribution

What it is, in one line: 3,000 skin disease terms written by dermatologists, on BioPortal
What it does: Our concerns (eczema, rosacea, acne) point at real clinical terms aligned to ICD-10
Why, or why not: Six lines of alignment fix the fact that no clinician has checked our vocabulary

What it is, in one line: Wikipedia's facts as a queryable graph
What it does: Tells us who owns each brand. L'Oreal owns 570 of our products
Why, or why not: One line per brand, and we get ownership and country for free

What it is, in one line: Wikipedia turned into a graph, older cousin of Wikidata
What it does: Abesova pulled countries and map coordinates from it
Why, or why not: Wikidata is better maintained now

What it is, in one line: Where biomedical ontologies live. OBO is the community with shared rules
What it does: DermO is on BioPortal. TOXIN reused TXPO from OBO
Why, or why not: We fetch DermO from here

What it is, in one line: A search engine for existing vocabulary terms
What it does: Search 'price' before inventing skc:price
Why, or why not: The one habit that separates an amateur ontology from a professional one

What it is, in one line: A free website that checks your ontology against 41 known design mistakes
What it does: Paste the file, get a graded list: critical, important, minor
Why, or why not: One afternoon for a real evaluation number nobody in group A has

What it is, in one line: A free website that scores how FAIR your ontology is (findable, accessible, interoperable, reusable)
What it does: 24 checks, a score, and what is missing
Why, or why not: We criticise everyone for not publishing, so we measure our own

What it is, in one line: Structural numbers: depth, breadth, richness
What it does: Comparable figures for the evaluation table
Why, or why not: Cheap and standard

What it is, in one line: Makes a documentation web page from the ontology file
What it does: So the docs cannot drift from the code
Why, or why not: Free, and it is what the w3id address will point at

What it is, in one line: A permanent web address for your ontology
What it does: Survives you leaving BAU. It is a pull request on GitHub
Why, or why not: A university URL dies when you graduate

What it is, in one line: Gives a DOI to each release
What it does: The ontology becomes citable like a paper
Why, or why not: One in six competitors publishes. This is how we do it properly

What it is, in one line: An older, document-heavy method: glossary, taxonomies, relation diagrams, concept dictionary
What it does: The default in this field. bit-Tech, Utari and Mahadewi all use it. Moe & Aung follow it without naming it
Why, or why not: Thorough but old. We take its glossary step and use MOMo + LOT instead, with a stated reason

What it is, in one line: Modular Ontology Modeling. Build in modules using design patterns, draw before you write
What it does: Our four-module design follows it
Why, or why not: Names four reasons reuse fails and we have hit three of them

What it is, in one line: Linked Open Terms. Four steps: requirements, build, publish, maintain
What it does: Our project structure and publication discipline
Why, or why not: Built around reusing terms and publishing, which are the two things this field is worst at

What it is, in one line: Noy & McGuinness 2001, the seven-step teaching guide
What it does: Its class-vs-individual test told us Annex entries are individuals
Why, or why not: Everyone cites it. Too light to be our only method

What it is, in one line: Questions the ontology must be able to answer, written BEFORE building
What it does: Our 15 questions become our 15 SPARQL queries become our evaluation chapter. COPPER did the same
Why, or why not: Turns 'is it good' into something measurable

Tool: THINGS THE PAPERS USED THAT WE DON'T

What it is, in one line: Conversational case-based reasoning. Narrow a problem by asking questions, like a doctor
What it does: Moe & Aung: six questions turn 'I have acne' into 'papules'
Why, or why not: Needs a hand-built case base and a dermatologist

What it is, in one line: A maximum-flow algorithm. Water through pipes
What it does: Moe & Aung score products by how much flow reaches them
Why, or why not: A weighted filter does the same for us with less machinery

What it is, in one line: Convolutional neural network, a model that reads images
What it does: Hansanie & Silva grade acne from a photo. Lee et al. read the face
Why, or why not: No photos, no ethics approval. Could plug in later

What it is, in one line: A neural net that passes messages between connected nodes
What it does: HaCKG predicts halal status with one
Why, or why not: Future work. Needs interaction data

What it is, in one line: Analytic Hierarchy Process. Weigh several criteria by comparing them in pairs
What it does: Formultools ranks ingredients on performance, origin and price with it
Why, or why not: Could rank products on price, availability and evidence. Not needed yet

What it is, in one line: Standard questionnaires for user experience and usability
What it does: Formultools used AttrakDiff between iterations. Mahadewi reported SUS 82
Why, or why not: If we ever build an interface. Cheap and standard

What it is, in one line: Standard accuracy measures
What it does: Moe & Aung, Hansanie, E-Prod and Mahadewi all report some of these
Why, or why not: FEVR says match the evaluation to the goal. Ours is verifiable correctness, so competency questions and consistency instead

What it is, in one line: A simple collaborative filtering algorithm
What it does: Mahadewi predicts ratings with it
Why, or why not: Needs a ratings matrix we do not have

What it is, in one line: A text way of writing a molecule's structure
What it does: TOXIN adds it so every chemical has one identity
Why, or why not: We have CAS numbers from CosIng, same job

What it is, in one line: The ToXic Process Ontology from OBO Foundry
What it does: TOXIN's backbone ontology
Why, or why not: Too deep into toxicology mechanisms for us
